Old town (Parte Vieja) classics and what to order:
- Gandarias (31 de Agosto 23): solomillo (sirloin) pintxo, plus a wide hot counter.
- La Cuchara de San Telmo (31 de Agosto 28, tucked behind the San Telmo museum): hot pintxos made to order: beef cheek (carrillera) in red wine, seared foie with apple.
- Borda Berri (Fermín Calbetón 12): hot dishes to order: beef cheek, Idiazabal cheese risotto, pig's ear.
- Ganbara (San Jerónimo 21): sautéed wild mushrooms with egg yolk, crab tartlet (txangurro).
- Txepetxa (Pescadería 5): marinated anchovies with toppings.
- Bar Néstor (Pescadería 11): the tortilla (cut only at about 13:00 and 20:00; put your name on the list at the bar about an hour before), tomato salad, txuleta steak.
- Atari (Mayor 18, by Santa María church): good pintxos and drinks on the plaza.
- La Viña (31 de Agosto 3): finish with the famous baked cheesecake.
Also: the Gilda (olive, anchovy, guindilla pepper) is on most counters.

Cost: cold counter pintxos are about €3-5. Hot ones made to order are about €4-8 (more for foie or steak). A zurito (small beer) or txakoli is about €2-3, and a glass of wine €2.50-4. A typical round of one pintxo and one drink is about €6-10 per person per bar. Four or five bars comes to roughly €35-50 each.

Tips: get there from about 19:30-20:00 (it's busiest from 20:30-22:00). Order one or two things per bar and move on. Tell the bartender what you had and pay at the end. Order hot pintxos from the chalkboard, because they're better than the counter ones. Many bars close one day a week, so check the night you go.

reference:
A good one-day loop (all walkable, about 3-4 km):
1. Markt (by 9:30): climb the Belfry, 366 steps, with views over the town. Tickets are about €15 and timed slots are best booked ahead.
2. Burg square, next door: the Basilica of the Holy Blood and the Gothic town hall.
3. Rozenhoedkaai: the classic canal view, and the main boat departure point.
4. Church of Our Lady, for Michelangelo's Madonna and Child. Across the street is St John's Hospital, with the Memling paintings. If you prefer Flemish art, go to the Groeninge Museum (Van Eyck) instead.
5. Lunch, or a beer and tour at De Halve Maan brewery (Walplein).
6. Begijnhof (béguinage), a quiet whitewashed courtyard, then Minnewater (the "Lake of Love").
7. Late afternoon: Jan van Eyckplein and Spiegelrei, a quieter canal area. Or walk out to the windmills on the Kruisvest ramparts.
Treats: frites from the stalls on the Markt, chocolate (The Chocolate Line or Dumon), waffles.

Is the canal boat worth it? Yes, for a first visit. It lasts about 30 minutes and costs €15 per adult (less for children; the price is set to rise to €17 in 2027). Boats are walk-up from several jetties (Rozenhoedkaai, Dijver, Katelijnestraat) and run daily from about 10:00 to 18:00 from March to mid-November. You see bridges, gardens and facades that you can't reach on foot. Go early, or try the Dijver or Katelijnestraat jetties, to skip the longest queues. Boats run in light rain but may not run in storms, high winds or freezing weather.

Yes, it's worth a morning, if you go early. It's one of the world's biggest markets: about 15,000 stalls in 27 sections.

Days and hours:
- Saturday and Sunday, about 9:00-18:00. This is the full market; many stalls are open by around 10:00.
- Friday 18:00-24:00: a smaller night session, mostly clothing wholesale.
- Wednesday and Thursday 7:00-18:00: plants and flowers only.
Go at 9:00-11:00, before the heat and the crowds peak.

Getting there: MRT Kamphaeng Phet (exit 2 opens right into the market), MRT Chatuchak Park, or BTS Mo Chit. The clock tower in the middle is the easy meeting point.

Good buys:
- Thai handicrafts, wood carvings, lacquerware, silk cushion covers, celadon and blue-and-white ceramics, benjarong porcelain.
- Home decor and lamps.
- Soaps and aromatherapy oils, coconut-wax candles.
- Vintage clothes, sneakers and denim (sections 5-6), cheap cotton clothes and elephant pants, local designer shops.
- Art and prints, antiques (sections 25-26; Buddha images need an export licence).
- Plants.
Eat there: coconut ice cream served in the shell, mango sticky rice, grilled pork skewers, fresh juices. Or Tor Kor fresh market is just across the road by Kamphaeng Phet.

Tips: carry cash in small notes and bargain politely (10-20% off is normal). Wear light clothes and drink plenty. Watch your bag in crowds, and keep a map photo, since getting lost is easy.

reference:
With kids aged 5 and 8, Monti is usually the best all-round base. Prati (near the Vatican) is the calmer second choice. Trastevere is the most fun but the noisiest at night.

- Monti: you can walk to the Colosseum, Forum and Trevi. It has a village feel (Piazza Madonna dei Monti and its fountain), easy pizza and gelato, and is close to Termini and metro lines A and B. Some streets are steep and cobbled, so bring a stroller only if needed.
- Prati/Vatican: flat, wide streets, quieter evenings, supermarkets, and the metro A line. It's handy for St Peter's, Castel Sant'Angelo and the Gianicolo. It's further from the ancient sites, so you'll take the metro or taxis more.
- Trastevere: cobbled lanes, great food, and a playground on Piazza San Cosimato. But bars are loud until late, and it has no metro (tram 8 and buses only). If you choose it, stay on a quiet side street or near Viale di Trastevere.

What kids enjoy:
- The Colosseum and Forum, ideally on a short family tour or with the underground/arena add-on.
- Throwing a coin in Trevi, the Pantheon dome, the Mouth of Truth, and Piazza Navona's fountains.
- Castel Sant'Angelo's ramparts.
- St Peter's dome climb. The 8-year-old will like it; take the lift for part of it. Keep the Vatican Museums short and book the first slot.
- Villa Borghese: rent bikes or a rickshaw, row a boat on the lake, and visit the Bioparco zoo.
- Explora children's museum (Via Flaminia 82; timed entry, closed Mondays, book ahead).
- Gianicolo hill: the noon cannon, and the free Pulcinella puppet show on weekends.
- Gelato daily, pizza al taglio, and a half-day trip to Ostia Antica.

field_atlas_141: The sound of your own voice when played back from a recording is primarily attributed to cognitive dissonance between a person's perception and expectation for the sound of their own voice [S1]. Because you normally hear yourself through two routes, and a recording only captures one.
- Air conduction: sound leaves your mouth and reaches your ears through the air, like anyone else's voice.
- Bone conduction: your vocal cords also vibrate your skull, jaw and the fluid of your inner ear directly. Bone and tissue carry low frequencies best, so this route adds bass and resonance.
Your "inner" voice is the blend, so it sounds deeper and fuller to you than it really is. A recording only picks up the air-conducted sound, which is what everyone else hears, so it sounds thinner, higher and unfamiliar.
There is a psychological part too: you have heard the blended version all your life, so the recording breaks expectation. Studies (e.g. Holzman & Rousey, 1966) found people feel discomfort hearing their recorded voice, yet when they unknowingly rate their own recorded voice among others, they often rate it more attractive than listeners do.
Also, while you speak your middle-ear muscles slightly damp your own voice, and cheap phone microphones and speakers cut bass, which makes recordings sound even tinnier.
The recording is closer to how others hear you.

Pressurisation: jet engines have compressors that squeeze outside air. A little of this hot, compressed "bleed air" is taken off the engines (the Boeing 787 uses electric compressors instead), cooled in air-conditioning packs, and pumped into the sealed fuselage. Pressure is controlled by an outflow valve near the tail that opens or closes to let air out at a set rate, so fresh air keeps flowing through.
At 11,000 m the outside pressure is only about 23 kPa (under a quarter of sea level). The cabin is kept at a "cabin altitude" of no more than 8,000 ft (2,440 m) by regulation, about 75 kPa (roughly 0.75 atmosphere). Newer jets (787, A350) hold about 6,000 ft. Full sea-level pressure would need a heavier, more stressed fuselage.
Why the bottle crumples: if you drank and recapped it during cruise, it is sealed with cabin air at about 75 kPa. On descent the cabin pressure rises back to about 101 kPa at the ground. Air outside pushes harder than the air inside: 101 / 75 = about 1.35 times, so the trapped air is squeezed to roughly 75 percent of its volume (Boyle's law) and the soft plastic dents in. The reverse happens on climb: a bottle sealed on the ground bulges and crisp packets puff up. Your ears pop for the same reason.

The burn: chillies contain capsaicin. It binds to a receptor on your pain nerves called TRPV1, which normally fires for heat above about 43 C. Capsaicin switches it on chemically, so your brain gets a genuine "burning" signal even though no tissue is being burned. That is why you sweat, flush and your nose runs: your body is trying to cool down from heat that isn't there.
Why water doesn't help: capsaicin is an oily, fat-soluble molecule that barely dissolves in water. Water just washes over it and spreads it around your mouth, while the capsaicin stays stuck to the receptors.

Cold milk also soothes. Whole milk, yoghurt, lassi, sour cream or ice cream all work; studies have found milk beats water and sugar water roughly halves the burn too.
Other options: rice, bread or tortillas soak up and scrub off the oil; sugar or honey help a bit. Alcohol dissolves capsaicin but beer is mostly water so it does little.
Repeated eating desensitises TRPV1 nerves, which is why regular chilli eaters tolerate more.

A satellite phone works by connecting to the public switched telephone network (PSTN) through orbiting satellites instead of terrestrial cell towers [S1]. It requires a clear view of the sky because normal phones rely on cell towers for signal, while satellite phones need line-of-sight to a satellite to transmit voice, text, and low-bandwidth data [S1].

Geostationary satellites appear fixed in the sky, allowing near-global coverage with few satellites [S2]. However, the long signal path introduces latency but supports higher data throughput than LEO networks [S2]. Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites orbit Earth every 70–100 minutes and require constellations of dozens of satellites to provide continuous service [S3].

The orbit determines coverage area, latency, and terminal design [S6]. Early handsets required deployable antennas, while later models are comparable in size to ordinary smartphones [S4]. Fixed ship and vehicle installations use directional microwave antennas that track satellites automatically [S4]. Smaller systems may rely on VoIP over satellite internet links such as BGAN or VSAT [S4]. Indoor reception is limited and may require external antennas or repeaters [S4]. More recently, unmodified smartphones with no special support for satellite communication are also able to be used for direct-to-phone satellite telephony [S4].

The first voice signals relayed via satellite were transmitted in 1958 using the experimental SCORE satellite [S5]. MARISAT (1976) became the first dedicated mobile communications satellite and was later integrated into the Inmarsat organization, founded in 1979 [S5].

Sources disagree on the specific number of active satellites for some systems: Globalstar has 48 active satellites, while Iridium has 66 active near-polar satellites [S3]. Both systems launched in the late 1990s, experienced bankruptcy, and were later restructured [S3].

- Iridium: 66 active satellites in low orbit about 780 km up, covering the whole planet including the poles; they hand your call from satellite to satellite as they pass overhead.
- Inmarsat and Thuraya: a few geostationary satellites about 35,786 km above the equator, covering most of the world except the polar regions; you must face the satellite's part of the sky.
Why it needs a clear sky: the satellite is hundreds to tens of thousands of kilometres away and the phone only transmits about 1 watt, so the signal arriving is extremely weak. Satellite phones use L-band microwaves (about 1.6 GHz), which travel in straight lines and are absorbed or blocked by roofs, walls, dense trees, canyon walls and even your body. There's no nearby tower to bounce signal around obstacles, so the antenna needs line of sight. Best practice: go outside, extend the antenna vertically, stand clear of buildings, and give it a minute to lock on.
Newer smartphones with satellite SOS or texting (e.g. iPhone 14 and later, recent Pixel and Galaxy models, carrier direct-to-cell services) follow the same rule: outdoors, clear view of the sky, and point the phone as the screen guides.

Night cramps after a big walking day are most likely caused by tired muscles, not a lack of minerals. Fatigue upsets the balance between the nerve signals that tell a muscle to contract and those that tell it to relax, so the calf or foot fires off on its own, often when your foot points down under the bedding (which shortens the calf). question: How does an electric kettle know when the water is boiling and switch itself off?
field_atlas_141: An electric kettle switches off when a bimetallic thermostat flexes due to steam, which activates a bimetallic strip that cuts off the current [S2].
field_atlas_142: An electric kettle switches off when a bimetallic thermostat flexes due to steam, which activates a bimetallic strip that cuts off the current [S2].
reference:
Most electric kettles use a small bimetallic switch, usually made by Strix, and steam.
1. A bimetallic disc is made of two metals bonded together that expand at different rates when heated. When it reaches a set temperature it suddenly snaps from curved one way to curved the other way, with a click.
2. That disc sits at the back of the kettle near the handle, at the end of a small tube or channel that runs from inside the kettle.
3. While the water is only hot, little steam reaches the disc. When the water boils hard, a burst of steam is forced up through the channel and onto the disc.
4. The disc heats up, snaps over and pushes a lever that opens the electrical contacts, switching off the element. The "click" and the switch flicking off is that movement.
This is why a kettle switches off at boiling even at high altitude where water boils below 100 C, and why it won't switch off if the lid is open (steam escapes instead of going to the sensor).
There is also a second safety switch under the element: if you switch the kettle on empty, it overheats and a separate bimetallic cut-out trips to stop the element burning out.
Many newer kettles with temperature settings use an electronic temperature sensor (thermistor) and a microchip instead of a steam switch, cutting power when the chosen temperature is reached.

_Altitude sickness: shown as published by National Park Service (Rocky Mountain NP) [S1]._

Every year, rangers in Rocky Mountain National Park treat countless park visitors with headaches, nausea, dizziness, and a host of other ailments. Many of the people they are treating are suffering from Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS), a generic label applied to symptoms commonly experienced by people visiting high altitudes. The people treated by the rangers aren’t all rock climbers and mountaineers. Many of them are simply enjoying an easy hike or leisurely drive through the park with their family or friends. When travelling above 8,000 feet, everyone is susceptible to AMS.

As a person ascends through the atmosphere, every breath contains fewer and fewer molecules of oxygen. The body’s efforts to compensate for the reduced atmospheric pressure and a lower concentration of oxygen result in the symptoms associated with AMS. In order to avoid worsening symptoms, learn to recognize early signs of AMS.

Symptoms of mild AMS include mild headaches, increased breathing, rapid pulse, nausea, loss of appetite, lack of energy, and general malaise. These are warning signs not to go any higher than you already are.

A person suffering from moderate AMS may begin vomiting, experiencing increased shortness of breath and a headache that doesn’t respond to typical pain relievers. If you or someone you are travelling with experience these symptoms, it is important to descend to lower elevations immediately. Spend at least a day at an elevation where you are comfortable before attempting to ascend again.

If symptoms advance to a lack of balance or coordination, slurring of words, altered mental state, extreme shortness of breathe, a wet or rasping cough, or blue skin, the person may be experiencing severe AMS and their life may be in jeopardy. Go down immediately and seek medical attention.

The easiest way to treat AMS is to prevent it. Remember these simple rules when travelling to altitude. When travelling to high altitude (above 10,000 feet), it is wise to spend at least one night at a moderate elevation before ascending. Climb as high as you like during the day but never spend the night more than 1,000 feet higher than the night before. Remember that if you’re thirsty, you’re already dehydrated. Drink water often. Never take a headache with you when ascending. Treat the headache before going any higher. If you can’t treat it, you’re already too high.

Fortunately, AMS is extremely easy to treat if diagnosed in time. The most effective treatment is simply to GO DOWN.

Going up slowly is the main prevention and works for most people; Diamox (acetazolamide) is a useful back-up, worth taking if your schedule is fast or you've had altitude sickness before.

Look at the fin, the head and the behaviour.
- Dorsal fin: most dolphins have a tall, curved, hooked (falcate) fin that sweeps back. Porpoises have a small, low triangular fin, like a shark's but smaller.

Take lithium AA (lithium iron disulfide, for example Energizer Ultimate Lithium).
- Cold performance: lithium AAs are rated to work down to about -40 C. Alkaline batteries lose much of their capacity below 0 C and can deliver only a fraction of their power around -20 C, so your headlamp dims or switches off early.
- Capacity under load: lithium cells hold voltage better at the higher current a headlamp draws, so you get brighter light for longer.
- Weight: about 15 g each vs about 23 g for alkaline, which helps if you carry spares.
- Leaks and storage: lithium doesn't leak like alkaline and lasts up to 20 years on the shelf.
- Cost: they cost about 2 to 3 times more, but in the cold they outlast alkaline by much more, so they're the better value for this trip.
Check: make sure your headlamp accepts 1.5 V lithium AAs (almost all do). Don't use 3.7 V lithium-ion cells (14500 size) unless the manufacturer says it can take them.
Cold-weather tips: carry spare batteries in an inside pocket close to your body, keep the headlamp in your sleeping bag at night, and if your headlamp has a separate battery pack, run it under your jacket. Sake and soju are different kinds of drink, not two versions of the same thing.

Sake (Japan)
- Made by brewing polished rice with koji mould and yeast, the way beer is brewed. It is not distilled.
- Usually 15-16% ABV. Undiluted genshu is about 17-20%. The legal maximum is 22%.
- Tastes soft, rice-like, fruity or dry, much like a wine.

Soju (Korea)
- A distilled spirit, usually made from rice, wheat, barley or tapioca/sweet potato starch.
- The common green-bottle brands are now about 15.7-16.5%. Chamisul Fresh dropped to 15.7% in June 2026, and Jinro to 15.7% earlier in 2026. "Original" versions run about 20%. Traditional distilled soju such as Andong soju is 20-45%.

reference:
Rise (1602-c.1670)
- Founded in 1602 when the Dutch government merged rival trading firms into the Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC). It got a 21-year monopoly on Dutch trade east of the Cape of Good Hope.
- New financing: anyone could buy shares, the capital was permanent and the shares traded on the Amsterdam exchange. It is often called the first modern listed company, and it could raise huge sums cheaply.
- State-like powers: it could wage war, make treaties, build forts, mint coins and run colonies. Jan Pieterszoon Coen founded Batavia (Jakarta) in 1619 as its Asian headquarters.
- It took monopolies by force: nutmeg and mace through the conquest of the Banda Islands in 1621, which killed or expelled most Bandanese, then cloves in the Moluccas. It drove out the Portuguese and the English, held Ceylon and Malacca, and was the only Western trader allowed in Japan (Dejima).
- Dutch shipping, Amsterdam finance and the Asian "country trade" between Asian ports made it the world's biggest company. Around 1670 it had about 150 merchant ships, 40 warships, 50,000 employees and 10,000 soldiers. Dividends averaged about 18% a year.

Decline and bankruptcy (1700s)
- Spice profits fell as tastes moved to tea, coffee and textiles, where the VOC had no monopoly. The British East India Company was more competitive.
- Forts, garrisons and wars cost more and more.
- Staff were badly paid, and smuggling, private trade and corruption were rampant ("VOC" was joked to mean "Vergaan Onder Corruptie", "perished by corruption").

Why Norway is rich
- It was already a stable, high-trust democracy with good institutions, hydropower, shipping and fisheries before oil was found (Ekofisk, 1969).
- The state captures most of the oil money through a 78% marginal tax on petroleum profits (22% corporate plus 56% special tax). It also has direct stakes in fields (the SDFI) and majority ownership of Equinor (about 67%).

How the fund works
- The Government Pension Fund Global, set up in 1990 with first money paid in in 1996, receives the state's net oil and gas income. It is run by Norges Bank Investment Management.
- It invests only abroad: about 70% shares (around 1.5% of all the world's listed companies), plus bonds, property and renewable infrastructure.

### Symptoms

The major symptoms of a heart attack are:

- Chest pain or discomfort. Most heart attacks involve discomfort in the center or left side of the chest that lasts for more than a few minutes or that goes away and comes back. The discomfort can feel like uncomfortable pressure, squeezing, fullness, or pain.
- Feeling weak, light-headed, or faint. You may also break into a cold sweat.
- Pain or discomfort in the jaw, neck, or back.
- Pain or discomfort in one or both arms or shoulders.
- Shortness of breath. This often comes along with chest discomfort, but shortness of breath also can happen before chest discomfort.

Other symptoms of a heart attack could include unusual or unexplained tiredness and nausea or vomiting. Women are more likely to have these other symptoms. Learn more about women and heart disease.

#### Call 9-1-1 if you notice symptoms of a heart attack

If you notice the symptoms of a heart attack in yourself or someone else, call 9-1-1 immediately. The sooner you get to an emergency room, the sooner you can get treatment to reduce the amount of damage to the heart muscle. At the hospital, health care professionals can run tests to find out if a heart attack is happening and can decide the best treatment.

In some cases, a heart attack requires cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) or an electrical shock (defibrillation) to the heart to get the heart pumping again. Bystanders trained to use CPR or a defibrillator may be able to help until emergency medical personnel arrive.

Short answer: for most people, ordinary fish-oil capsules (about 1 g a day) have not been shown to prevent heart attacks. One high-dose prescription form of purified EPA helps a specific high-risk group.

Big trials
- ASCEND (2018, 15,480 people with diabetes, 1 g/day): no reduction in serious vascular events.
- VITAL (2018, 25,871 healthy US adults, 1 g/day): no significant drop in the main outcome (heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death). Heart attacks were about 28% lower as a secondary finding, which counts only as a hint.
- REDUCE-IT (2018, 8,179 people on statins with raised triglycerides and heart disease or diabetes, 4 g/day icosapent ethyl, i.e. pure EPA): major cardiovascular events fell about 25% (17.2% vs 22.0%). Critics say the mineral-oil placebo may have raised risk in the comparison group.
- STRENGTH (2020, 13,078 similar patients, 4 g/day EPA+DHA): stopped early with no benefit.
- OMEMI (2021, older people after a heart attack, 1.8 g/day): no benefit.
- The Cochrane review (2020, 86 trials): little or no effect on deaths or cardiovascular events overall.

Harms
- High doses raise the risk of atrial fibrillation (REDUCE-IT 5.3% vs 3.9%). A large UK Biobank study (BMJ Medicine, 2024) linked regular fish-oil use in healthy people to about 13% more AF and 5% more stroke.

What this means
- Eat oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) about twice a week rather than relying on capsules.
- If you have heart disease and high triglycerides despite a statin, ask a doctor about prescription icosapent ethyl (Vascepa/Vazkepa). Over-the-counter capsules are not a substitute.
- Statins, blood-pressure control, not smoking and exercise prevent far more heart attacks.

reference:
Why they're still rising
- The Indian plate is still moving north into Asia at about 4-5 cm a year. About 2 cm a year of that is squeezed up across Nepal's Himalaya, and the rest is taken up in Tibet and beyond.
- India slides under Nepal along a huge, gently dipping fault, the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT). Crust stacks up and thickens above it, which lifts the mountains.
- GPS shows Everest rising about 2 mm a year. A 2024 study suggests part of that is rebound, because the Arun River has eroded away a lot of rock nearby. Erosion and landslides strip material at the same time, so the net height gain is slow.

The link to Nepal's big earthquakes
- The shallow part of the MHT (down to about 15-20 km) is locked. India keeps pushing, so strain builds for centuries, about 2 m per century.
- Eventually the fault slips suddenly, and that is a great earthquake. Recent ones were in 1255, 1505 (western Nepal, about M8+), 1934 (Bihar-Nepal M8.0) and 25 April 2015 (Gorkha M7.8, about 9,000 deaths).
- In 2015 the fault slipped about 4-6 m under a 150 km stretch from Gorkha to east of Kathmandu. Kathmandu was lifted about 1 m. The high peaks just to the north dropped about 0.6 m in places (Everest itself fell only a few cm), because they sit where the crust had been elastically bent.
- So the mountains go up slowly between earthquakes and partly settle back during them. Over many cycles they gain a little permanent height.

What it means now
- The 2015 rupture didn't reach the surface and didn't release the strain in the west. Western Nepal (a gap since 1505) and the zone west of Kathmandu are still loaded, and another M8 is expected there sometime, with no way to predict when. Building codes and earthquake drills matter.

question: how did japan go from a closed feudal country to an industrial power in just a few decades after the meiji restoration?

reference:
Japan went from feudal isolation to an industrial and military power in about 40 years (1868 to around 1905). Five things drove it.

1. Shock and urgency. US Commodore Perry's warships (1853-54) forced unequal treaties, and China's humiliation by Britain was a warning. Reformist samurai from Satsuma and Choshu overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate in 1868 in the name of the Meiji emperor, under the slogan "rich country, strong army" (fukoku kyohei).

2. Tearing down feudalism fast:
- 1871: the domains (han) were abolished and replaced with prefectures run from Tokyo.
- 1873: a national conscription army replaced the samurai, and a fixed money land tax gave the state steady income.
- 1876: samurai stipends were ended. The Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 was crushed.

3. Copying the West selectively. The Iwakura Mission (1871-73) studied the US and Europe. Japan hired about 3,000 foreign experts (oyatoi), sent students abroad, and chose what worked: a British-style navy, a German-style army and constitution (1889), and French-influenced law and schools.

4. The state built industry, then handed it over. Japan's first railway (Tokyo-Yokohama) and the Tomioka silk mill opened in 1872, along with telegraphs, mines, shipyards and the Bank of Japan (1882). From 1880 the state sold its factories cheaply to business groups (zaibatsu) such as Mitsui and Mitsubishi. Silk and textile exports paid for imported machines.

5. Strong Edo-era foundations. Literacy was high, with roughly 40% of boys schooled. There were commercial networks, the Osaka rice exchange, large cities, and a disciplined administrative class. Compulsory education from 1872 built on this.

Results: Japan defeated China (1894-95) and Russia (1904-05), ended the unequal treaties (1899-1911) and annexed Korea (1910). The costs: heavy taxes on peasants, harsh factory labour, and a militarism that led on to imperial expansion.

How to check:
1. Copy the transaction hash (0x… plus 64 hex characters) from your wallet's activity list. Most wallets have a "View on block explorer" link.
2. Open etherscan.io and paste it into the search bar. If you only have your address, search for that and open the transaction from the list.
3. Look at the "Status" field. Also check "Block", the number of "Block Confirmations", "Transaction Fee", and the From, To and Value fields. For tokens, check "ERC-20 Tokens Transferred".

What the statuses mean:
- Pending: the transaction has been broadcast but is not yet in a block. Usually the gas fee was set too low for current demand. It costs nothing until it is mined. Wait, or use your wallet's "Speed up" (same nonce, higher fee) or "Cancel" (a 0 ETH transaction to yourself with the same nonce).
- Success: it is in a block and executed. With a few confirmations it is final and cannot be reversed. Etherscan cannot undo it.
- Failed (red, often "execution reverted" or "out of gas"): it went into a block but the contract rejected it. Common causes are slippage, an expired deadline, a missing token approval, too low a gas limit, or a sold-out mint. Nothing was transferred: your tokens and ETH value stay with you.
- Dropped & Replaced: another transaction with the same nonce, such as a speed-up or cancel, was mined instead.
- Dropped / not found: the transaction left the mempool and never made it on chain.

Fees: yes, you lose the fee on a failed transaction. The validators did the work, so you pay for the gas used up to the point of failure. Only the fee is lost, not the amount you tried to send. Pending, dropped and replaced transactions that never reach a block cost nothing. For a replaced transaction you pay only the fee of the one that was mined.

- Keep only trading money on exchanges.
- Prefer regulated exchanges that segregate customer assets and publish audited proof of reserves. The EU's MiCA rules require segregation.
- Spread funds across more than one platform.

reference:
A timelock is a rule built into a Bitcoin transaction or script that keeps coins from being spent until a set time.

Types:
- Absolute timelock (nLockTime, OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY / BIP65): the coins can't be spent before a given date or block height, for example 1 January 2028.
- Relative timelock (OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY / BIP112): the coins can't be spent until N blocks after they were confirmed. One block is about 10 minutes, so 52,560 blocks is about 1 year. The maximum is 65,535 blocks, about 15 months.

The Bitcoin network enforces these rules itself. No company or lawyer needs to cooperate.

Using it for inheritance (a "dead man's switch"):
1. Set up a wallet with two spending paths. Path A: your key can spend at any time. Path B: your heir's key can spend, but only after the timelock, say 12 months of inactivity.
2. While you are alive, "refresh" the coins before the timer runs out by sending them to yourself in the same wallet. This restarts the clock, and your heir can never spend early.
3. If you die or lose your keys, the timer runs out and your heir signs with their own key. If you lose your own key, you can use the same path yourself.

Wallets that do this: Liana (desktop, works with Ledger, BitBox02, Jade, Coldcard and others), Nunchuk (decaying-multisig inheritance), and Bitcoin Keeper.

Essentials:
- Back up the wallet descriptor (the wallet's full spending policy) as well as the seeds. Without the descriptor your heir can't find or spend the coins.
- Give your heir their key, the descriptor and written step-by-step instructions, and test the whole process with a small amount first.
- Put a calendar reminder for refreshes well before expiry.
- A simpler, more fragile option: give your heir a pre-signed transaction with nLockTime set to a future date. It becomes invalid if you move the coins.
- Mention the arrangement in your will too.

question: what is a one-time pad and why do people say it's the only truly unbreakable encryption? why doesn't everyone use it
field_atlas_141:
A one-time pad (OTP) is a symmetric encryption technique that uses a single-use pre-shared key larger than or equal to the size of the message, combining it with the plaintext via modular addition or the exclusive or (XOR) operation. The resulting ciphertext is impossible to decrypt without the key, provided the key meets four conditions: it must be at least as long as the plaintext, it must be truly random, it must never be reused, and it must be kept completely secret [S1].

People say the OTP is the only encryption system mathematically proven to be unbreakable because, under information theory, if the key is truly random, used only once, and kept secret, the ciphertext provides absolutely no additional information about the plaintext; every possible plaintext of the same length is equally likely [S5]. This property is termed perfect secrecy [S1].

However, OTP is rarely used in practice because the primary challenge is secure key distribution. Since the key must be pre-shared and kept secret, distributing it securely between parties is extremely difficult, making the method impractical for many applications despite its theoretical security [S1]. Additionally, the OTP is rarely used today because failure to generate and share truly random keys has led to successful cryptanalysis, such as in the Venona project [S2].

reference:
A one-time pad (OTP) encrypts a message by combining it with a secret random key of the same length. In binary each bit is XORed with a key bit. With letters, each letter is shifted by a key letter mod 26. For example, H (7) + key X (23) = 30 mod 26 = 4 = E. Gilbert Vernam and Joseph Mauborgne developed it around 1917–19. In 1949 Claude Shannon proved it gives "perfect secrecy."

Why it can't be broken: given any ciphertext, every plaintext of the same length is equally likely. Some key would produce each one. "ATTACK" could just as well decrypt to "RETIRE" with a different key. The ciphertext leaks nothing except the length, so even unlimited computing power, including quantum computers, can't help.

This is true only if all four conditions hold:
1. The key is truly random, not from a pseudo-random generator.
2. The key is at least as long as the message.
3. The key is never reused. Reuse is fatal: Soviet pad reuse let the US Venona project decrypt thousands of messages.
4. The key stays completely secret and is destroyed after use.

Why almost nobody uses it:

- Key storage and sync: both sides must keep huge keys safe and perfectly in step.
- No integrity or authentication: an attacker can flip bits in the ciphertext and change the message undetected.
- Good randomness at scale is hard to produce.

field_atlas_141: The Parthenon was built between 447 BC and 432 BC during the reign of Pericles [S1]. It was originally a temple to honor the goddess Athena for nearly 900 years from the 5th century BC to the 5th century AD [S1].

The Parthenon was built between 447 and 438 BC, and its sculptural decoration was finished by 432 BC. This was the height of Classical Athens, under the statesman Pericles. It stands on the Acropolis in Athens, Greece.

Who built it: the architects were Iktinos (Ictinus) and Kallikrates (Callicrates). The sculptor Pheidias (Phidias) oversaw the artwork. It is a Doric temple of Pentelic marble, 8 × 17 columns, about 69.5 × 30.9 m. Its subtle curves and leaning columns correct optical illusions. It replaced an older temple that the Persians destroyed in 480 BC.

What it was for:
- A temple to Athena Parthenos ("Athena the Virgin"), patron goddess of Athens. Its inner hall housed Pheidias's roughly 12 m gold-and-ivory statue of her (now lost).
- A treasury: it stored the city's wealth, including funds of the Delian League.
- A monument to Athens' victory over the Persians and to its power and wealth. Its frieze shows the Panathenaic procession, and the pediments show Athena's birth and her contest with Poseidon.
The main religious rituals of the Panathenaic festival focused on the older cult image in the nearby Erechtheion. The Parthenon was more a showpiece and votive offering than an ordinary place of worship.

Later history: it became a Christian church (from about the 6th century) and then an Ottoman mosque (after 1460s). In 1687 a Venetian shell ignited Ottoman gunpowder stored inside, which blew out the centre. Lord Elgin removed many sculptures in 1801–12. These "Parthenon Marbles" are in the British Museum, and Greece still seeks their return. Restoration is ongoing.

- Greenland: about 2.17 million km² (836,000 sq mi)
- Africa: about 30.3 million km² (11.7 million sq mi)

- About 3 times the size of Texas, or about 9 times the UK
- Still the world's largest island (Australia counts as a continent)
- Africa could hold the USA, China, India and much of Europe combined.

The Okavango Delta is in northwestern Botswana, in southern Africa. It lies around 19°S, 23°E, just north of the town of Maun, which is the main gateway.

What it is: one of the world's largest inland deltas. The Okavango River rises in the highlands of Angola and flows through Namibia's Zambezi (Caprivi) Strip. It then fans out across the flat Kalahari Desert instead of reaching the sea. The water spreads over roughly 6,000–15,000 km² of channels, lagoons, papyrus swamps and islands, depending on the season and the year, and almost all of it evaporates or soaks into the sand.

- Seasonal flood timing: Angola's summer rains (Nov–Mar) take months to arrive, so the flood peaks in Botswana's dry winter, around June–August. Animals crowd in from the surrounding desert just when water is scarce everywhere else.
- Wildlife: large elephant herds (Botswana has the world's largest elephant population, around 130,000), buffalo, hippos, crocodiles, lions, leopards, cheetahs, rare African wild dogs, rhinos, and red lechwe and sitatunga antelope. There are also over 400 bird species.
- UNESCO: it became the 1,000th World Heritage Site in June 2014.
- A wilderness safari model: low-volume, high-cost tourism. Visitors glide through the channels in a mokoro (dugout canoe), take game drives in Moremi Game Reserve, or fly over the delta by light aircraft from Maun.

The best game viewing is from about June to October.

Don Quixote was written by Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (1547–1616), the Spanish novelist, playwright and poet.

When:
- Part One, "El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha", was published in Madrid in early 1605 by the printer Juan de la Cuesta. Cervantes was 57. He may have conceived it while jailed in Seville around 1597–98.
- In 1614 an unauthorized sequel appeared under the pseudonym Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda.
- Part Two, "Segunda parte del ingenioso caballero don Quijote de la Mancha", was published in 1615, partly in response to that sequel, which Cervantes mocks in the book.
- Cervantes died in Madrid on 22 April 1616, the year after Part Two came out.

Why it matters: it is often called the first modern novel. It follows Alonso Quijano, a minor nobleman who reads so many chivalric romances that he renames himself Don Quixote. He sets out as a knight-errant with his down-to-earth squire Sancho Panza and his horse Rocinante, famously "tilting at windmills" he mistakes for giants. It is one of the best-selling and most translated works of fiction, and a cornerstone of Spanish literature, which is often called "the language of Cervantes."

Chefchaouen (also called Chaouen, or Xauen in Spanish) is Morocco's famous "Blue Pearl," a small mountain town whose medina is washed in shades of blue.

Basics:
- Location: in the Rif Mountains of northern Morocco, at about 600 m elevation. It is about 110 km south of Tangier and 60 km south of Tétouan. Population: about 46,000 (2024 census).
- Name: from the Berber for "look at the horns," after the two peaks above the town.
- History: founded in 1471 by Moulay Ali ben Rachid as a kasbah (fortress) against Portuguese raids. Muslims and Jews expelled from Spain after 1492 settled here. It was closed to most outsiders until Spanish troops arrived in 1920, and it was part of the Spanish protectorate until 1956.
- Why blue: the origin is disputed. Theories credit Jewish refugees (blue as a symbol of the sky and heaven), keeping mosquitoes away, keeping houses cool, or modern tourism. The painting spread widely in the 20th century, and residents still repaint regularly.

What to see and do:
- Wander the blue lanes and stairways of the medina
- Plaza Uta el-Hammam, the main square, with the 15th-century Kasbah (museum and garden) and the Grand Mosque
- Ras el-Maa spring and its washing area at the edge of town
- The Spanish Mosque viewpoint, a 30-minute walk uphill and best at sunset
- Talassemtane National Park, the Akchour waterfalls and God's Bridge (about 45 minutes by car)
- Local goat cheese, woven wool blankets, and tagines

Getting there: CTM and other buses run from Tangier (about 3 hours), Tétouan (about 1.5 hours) and Fes (about 4–5 hours). Grand taxis also run from Tétouan. The town is calm and walkable, though it is busy with day-trippers from mid-morning.
